name: Aaron Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm a talker, so stop me if I go on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at five and the first thing I do is check the AI dashboard on my phone: which cows the robots flagged overnight, the weather, the grass growth figures. Then I walk the cows, meet the team at half six, and split the nine of them between the dairy, the beef sheds and the arable. What I love is solving problems; what wears me out is head office meetings on video calls.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the farm and your home life.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ridgeway is 700 hectares, owned by a regional food company, with 400 dairy cows, a beef unit and wheat, barley and maize. I've managed it for eight years after a degree in agriculture. My partner Lena is a large-animal vet, and we've got Jonas, who's eleven, and Mia, who's eight, and a mortgage on a house in the next village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Now I'll read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. I use AI every day for grazing plans and feed budgets, and it's good, but I'd hoped for more. Online I'd probably post that the hype crowd owe farmers an apology, and then go back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job is safe and stays interesting. I run Ridgeway, a 700-hectare dairy, beef and cereal farm owned by a regional food company, and the tools I've got already save me an hour a day. My pay is good, Lena's a vet, and we've got solid savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the plan we've got: a third robotic milker next autumn, which the company has already signed off. I'd keep trialling the drone for crop scouting on the wheat. And I'd keep pushing the company to fund the team's tractor-driving and herd-health courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of restlessness. I like change, so a flat world bores me slightly. But nobody's going to cry for a well-paid farm manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tools save you an hour a day. What do you do with that hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I walk the fields, which is what I trained to do in the first place. The AI tells me which paddock the cows should graze tomorrow, and I go and check if it's right. The AI on my farm is right about four times in five, and the fifth time is why I still have a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team do you think about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta, who runs the robotic milkers. When we brought the first robot in, Marta was terrified she'd be out of work, and now she's the best robot technician in the county. In a quiet world she gets a pay rise and that's it.

say: I'd say I'm **disappointed**, because the AI I use daily is good but limited.
I'd post that the **hype crowd** owe farmers an apology.
think: I think my **job is safe** and stays interesting, with tools already saving time.
Good **pay**, Lena's vet income and **savings** make us secure.
do: Install a **third robotic milker** next autumn, already approved by the company.
Keep trialling the **drone** for scouting the wheat fields.
Push the company to fund the team's **training courses**.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **restlessness** at a world that stays flat.

fieldNote: He is an **early adopter** who already runs robotic milkers and daily AI planning.
He uses saved time to **walk the fields** and check the machine's advice.
He is proud of **Marta**, who moved from milker to robot technician.

steps.text: Install a third robotic milker next autumn
Keep running the farm and trialling the scouting drone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the world I've been getting ready for, and farms like ours are well placed. Online I'd say the gains should be shared with workers, not just shareholders, because that's where I stand. I'd also say hands-on farm work is safer for longer than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a lot of my job is planning and ordering, and that's the part this picture takes over. The company head office already wants one AI system planning feed and fertiliser across all its farms. I'd still be needed, but more as the person who checks the machine and leads the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this winter, I'd become the person in the company who knows the new planning system best, and I'd volunteer to roll it out on the other two farms. I'd add robot feed-pushers in the cattle shed by spring. And I'd sit down with the union rep and agree a written promise that no one on my team of nine goes without first being offered retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly, and a bit excited. I can see where I fit. My only worry is making sure the team comes with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're management, but you'd sit down with the union rep. Isn't that unusual?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but my dad lost his job at a sugar factory when I was a boy. Nobody sat down with my dad when the sugar factory automated, and he never really worked again. If I'm bringing in the machines, I want to be the one making sure people land somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonas, who's eleven, to learn how things work, not just how to use them. Jonas already takes apart the old radios in the shed. Mia is eight and wants to be a vet like her mum, which in this picture seems a pretty safe bet.

say: I'd say farms like ours are **well placed** for this change.
I'd say the **gains should be shared** with workers, not just shareholders.
think: I think the **planning and ordering** part of my job moves to software.
I'd become the person who **checks the machine** and leads the team.
do: Become the company's **expert** on the new planning system and roll it out.
Add **robot feed-pushers** in the cattle shed by spring.
Agree in writing with the union rep that everyone gets **retraining first**.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, with a clear sense of where he fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for rural jobs right now, not in five years. Online I'd argue for public ownership of the big AI systems, or at least strong rules, because two years is no time for anyone to prepare. I'd be loud about it, and I'd say it as someone who loves the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is in real danger by 2028. If an AI can plan every farm in the company better than me, head office needs one person per three farms, not one per farm. Then by 2031 the robots do the fieldwork and my team of nine shrinks to two or three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start this month by talking to the ag-tech firm that supplies our milkers about a job setting up robot systems on other farms. I'd push our savings from eight months to eighteen. I'd get the union and the company to agree redundancy terms for the team now, while there's goodwill. And I'd join the regional campaign for an AI dividend paid to rural communities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and that surprises me. I always thought I'd be on the winning side of this. Two years means even the people who saw it coming don't have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and the robots around 2031. What happens to you in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In those three years I'd be the guy installing the robots that will replace my own team, which is a strange job to have. The thinking part of my work goes first, so I'd be doing mostly hands-on setup and fixing. I'd probably be busy and well paid right up until the robots fix each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move to the ag-tech firm. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a real conversation I've already half had, honestly. The firm's area manager asked me last spring if I'd ever think about it. But I know that job only lasts as long as there are farms still being converted.

I'd argue for **public ownership** or strong rules for the big AI systems.

By 2031 the robots shrink my **team of nine** to two or three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the fast one, the rules matter most, but five years means we can get them right. I'd say farming can show other industries how to bring robots in fairly. I'd want our company to be the example.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to change my job before it changes me. By 2031 I'd want to be the person who designs how a robot farm runs, not the one being designed out. I think I'd come through fine, and I'd want my team to come through too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the agricultural robotics course at the university next September, evenings and weekends, about 4,000 which the company might pay. I'd turn Ridgeway into the company's test farm for robots. And on the side I'd start advising two or three neighbouring farms on robot milkers, for a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, like before a big harvest. There's work to do and time to do it. I'd rather this than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years before the robots mean for your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can train them properly. Marta becomes the robot lead, two of the younger lads train as technicians, and the older tractor drivers get a proper retirement deal. I'd want every name on the team to have a plan by 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're advising neighbours for a fee. Does that sit right with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, mostly, because I'd charge the big farms more and help the small ones cheaply. If I don't help the small farms, a corporate consultant will, and they'll sell them the wrong kit. I'd rather small farms get honest advice from someone who's done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make this a good thing for farming. We could have robots doing the back-breaking work and people doing the caring and the planning of landscapes. I'd say that with real hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm actually quite excited. Ten years is time to build something of my own, and with Lena's vet practice we could buy a smaller farm and run it with robots. I'd be 53 when the hands-on robots are good, which is a nice age to be the owner, not the employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running Ridgeway and saving, and look for 100 hectares to buy with Lena around 2030. I'd do the robotics course but take it slower. And I'd keep using AI every day, testing everything, because the people who know the tools best will set the terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly hopeful. It feels like the start of something, not the end. That's rare for me when people talk about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a farm and run it with robots. What does it look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like 100 hectares of mixed farming with robots doing the milking and weeding, and me and Lena doing the parts that need judgment. I'd want a farm school on it, where kids from town come to see how food is grown. Robots can't let a kid from town hold a lamb, and that's the bit of farming I'd build my own farm around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who don't have my options worry me. I've got savings, a degree and a partner with a good job, and most farm workers don't. If this decade is wasted, they'll be the ones who pay.

I'd say robots could take the **back-breaking work** while people do the caring.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even someone like me who's ready for change wouldn't have time to bring my team along. What would help is a law that makes companies agree retraining and redundancy terms before they bring in robots. And public money for farm workers to train as robot technicians, paid, not in their spare time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the data. Every cow on my farm generates information all day, and the company sells it to the feed firms. If AI runs farms, whoever owns the data owns farming.
